SECTION I
L	To be part of Zimbabwe’s “Born Free” generation was to be handed a promise: that your life
would no longer be shaped by colonial rule. Skin colour would not dictate the right to vote,
learn or work. For Simukai Chigudu, born in 1986, six years after independence, that promise
was stamped on him from the very beginning: “Your name, Simukai, it means to stand up,” his
father, a former liberation fighter, tells him.
Yet, as Chigudu reflects in his compelling memoir, the end of colonial rule does not mean
freedom from historical events and how they reverberate in everyday life. He tells two
interlinked stories: Zimbabwe’s brutal war of independence, and his own search for belonging
in the years that followed. It is a wide-ranging, restless book, passing through Uganda,
Rwanda, Ireland and Mexico City. Yet at its centre are Zimbabwe and Britain, “former colony
and metropole”, and the unfinished business between them.
Chigudu’s parents, who became part of the growing post-independence black middle class,
enrol him in elite private schools. There, he acquires what he calls a “delicate, papery accent”,
plays “white people’s sports” and learns the codes of respectability that promise safety but not
belonging. He comes to appreciate early on that to be black is to be defined by others. Black
Zimbabweans dismiss him as a “salad” for his adopted white habits (such as eating salad).
White Zimbabweans call him a soutpiel, or “salt penis”; for having one foot in Africa, one in
Europe, his genitals “[dangling] in the Mediterranean Sea”. In Britain, a student labels him
“the whitest black man” they know. The burden of his generation’s inheritance is expressed
most powerfully in descriptions of his grandfather’s murder — “they shot him in cold blood and
jettisoned his remains in a shallow pit” — and his father Tafi’s torture under the racist
Rhodesian government. Tafi joined the armed struggle and spent years in exile. “I felt the
weight of history, my life as the gift of his having survived colossal violence,” Chigudu writes.

would no longer be shaped by colonial rule. Skin colour would not dictate the right to vote,

father, a former liberation fighter, tells him.

freedom from historical events and how they reverberate in everyday life. He tells two
interlinked stories: Zimbabwe’s brutal war of independence, and his own search for belonging
in the years that followed. It is a wide-ranging, restless book, passing through Uganda,
Rwanda, Ireland and Mexico City. Yet at its centre are Zimbabwe and Britain, “former colony
and metropole”, and the unfinished business between them.

enrol him in elite private schools. There, he acquires what he calls a “delicate, papery accent”,

belonging. He comes to appreciate early on that to be black is to be defined by others. Black
Zimbabweans dismiss him as a “salad” for his adopted white habits (such as eating salad).

weight of history, my life as the gift of his having survived colossal violence,” Chigudu writes.

boulder, a hippo excretes in the face of another animal with the power of a missile, a crazed

Il.	In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I’ve been
turning over in my mind ever since.
‘Whenever you feel like criticizing any one,’ he told me, ‘just remember that all the people in
this world haven’t had the advantages that you've had.’
He didn’t say any more but we’ve always been unusually communicative in a reserved way,
and I understood that he meant a great deal more than that. In consequence I’m inclined to
reserve all judgments, a habit that has opened up many curious natures to me and also made
me the victim of not a few veteran bores. The abnormal mind is quick to detect and attach
itself to this quality when it appears in a normal person, and so it came about that in college I
was unjustly accused of being a politician, because I was privy to the secret griefs of wild,
unknown men. Most of the confidences were unsought—frequently I have feigned sleep,
preoccupation, or a hostile levity when I realized by some unmistakable sign that an intimate
revelation was quivering on the horizon—for the intimate revelations of young men or at least
the terms in which they express them are usually plagiaristic and marred by obvious
suppressions. Reserving judgments is a matter of infinite hope. I am still a little afraid of
missing something if I forget that, as my father snobbishly suggested, and I snobbishly repeat
a sense of the fundamental decencies is parcelled out unequally at birth.
And, after boasting this way of my tolerance, I come to the admission that it has a limit.
Conduct may be founded on the hard rock or the wet marshes but after a certain point I don’t
care what it’s founded on. When I came back from the East last autumn I felt that I wanted
the world to be in uniform and at a sort of moral attention forever; I wanted no more riotous
excursions with privileged glimpses into the human heart. Only Gatsby, the man who gives
his name to this book, was exempt from my reaction—Gatsby who represented everything for
which I have an unaffected scorn. [Word Count: 364]

Il.	In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I’ve been
turning over in my mind ever since.
‘Whenever you feel like criticizing any one,’ he told me, ‘just remember that all the people in
this world haven’t had the advantages that you've had.’
He didn’t say any more but we’ve always been unusually communicative in a reserved way,
and I understood that he meant a great deal more than that. In consequence I’m inclined to
reserve all judgments, a habit that has opened up many curious natures to me and also made
me the victim of not a few veteran bores. The abnormal mind is quick to detect and attach
itself to this quality when it appears in a normal person, and so it came about that in college I
was unjustly accused of being a politician, because I was privy to the secret griefs of wild,
unknown men. Most of the confidences were unsought—frequently I have feigned sleep,
preoccupation, or a hostile levity when I realized by some unmistakable sign that an intimate
revelation was quivering on the horizon—for the intimate revelations of young men or at least
the terms in which they express them are usually plagiaristic and marred by obvious
suppressions. Reserving judgments is a matter of infinite hope. I am still a little afraid of
missing something if I forget that, as my father snobbishly suggested, and I snobbishly repeat
a sense of the fundamental decencies is parcelled out unequally at birth.
And, after boasting this way of my tolerance, I come to the admission that it has a limit.
Conduct may be founded on the hard rock or the wet marshes but after a certain point I don’t
care what it’s founded on. When I came back from the East last autumn I felt that I wanted
the world to be in uniform and at a sort of moral attention forever; I wanted no more riotous
excursions with privileged glimpses into the human heart. Only Gatsby, the man who gives
his name to this book, was exempt from my reaction—Gatsby who represented everything for
which I have an unaffected scorn. [Word Count: 364]

threatened with extinction. Since 1970, more than half our flowering plants have decreased in
areas where they once thrived. In the 1950s, Britain’s hedgehog population was 30m strong.
Now, it is believed to be under a million. All this demands action. The problem is that a lot of
the action we’ve taken — mainly in the form of legislation — fails to target the biggest drivers of
nature loss. Instead, it bites when we try to build: wind turbines, solar farms, railways or
nuclear power plants, making their construction lengthier, more expensive or, in some cases,
impossible.

need more of in order to reduce reliance on fossil fuels, which ultimately cause habitat loss on
a massive scale. Greening the grid and providing clean electricity to homes, transport and
industry is one of the most urgent tasks facing us. The only way to do it without generating a
cost-of-living crisis that would dwarf our current predicament (and cause an anti-green
backlash) is to get building — and fast. At the moment, that’s proving far too difficult — and the
obstacles include those well-intentioned laws designed to guard habitats against unchecked

During an ongoing Lok Sabha election, the Commission issues a direction requiring candidates
to disclose AI-generated campaign videos and adds a 24-hour “verification window” before such
content can be shared. No statute or rule specifically covers AI videos. A candidate challenges
the direction as law-making, arguing only Parliament can regulate campaigning. The
Commission argues the measure is needed to ensure free and fair polls and fill a legislative
gap.
Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
Commission lacks power because only Parliament may fill gaps, so any direction without
explicit law is ultra vires today alone.

options.label: b
options.text:
Direction is invalid because electoral instructions must follow statutory rules, and silence
means prohibition, not permission, for regulators always here.

options.label: c
options.text:
Commission may act under superintendence, direction and control to conduct free and fair
elections and issue directions where law silent.

options.label: d
options.text:
Direction is valid only if approved by High Court beforehand, since administrative bodies
cannot expand powers without judicial sanction first.

than later petitions always anyway.

matters, which lie exclusively with Supreme Court alone always.

citizen group writes to the national Commission seeking countermanding and re-poll, citing its
expertise and national role. The national Commission replies that local body elections are
outside its mandate and advises approaching the State authority. The group files a petition
claiming the national Commission must administer every election in India to ensure
uniformity.
Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
Commission must intervene because municipal elections affect democracy, and Article 324
powers extend to every electoral body nationwide without exception.

options.label: b
options.text:
Commission does not conduct elections to Panchayats and Municipalities, because separate
State Election Commissions exist for those bodies in India.

options.label: c
options.text:
Commission must act because it administers all elections, and any local poll is part of
parliamentary process too always here.

options.label: d
options.text:
Commission cannot act because municipal polls are civil matters, and only civil courts
supervise them, not election bodies at all.

questions.stem:
During elections, the three-member Commission considers whether to suspend a recognised
party’s symbol for repeated Model Code violations. Two Election Commissioners vote to
suspend; the Chief Election Commissioner dissents and issues a press note stating his view
will “override” the majority because he heads the body. The party relies on the press note and
challenges the suspension as invalid, claiming the majority decision cannot stand.
Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
Decision stands because decisions are taken by majority, and the Chief Election
Commissioner has no overriding power over the others.

options.label: b
options.text:
Decision fails because Chief Election Commissioner is chair, so his dissent nullifies any
majority view automatically every time in law.

options.label: c
options.text:
Decision stands only if unanimous, because electoral fairness requires consensus, and split
votes show bias and invalidity always for citizens.

options.label: d
options.text:
Decision fails because dissent triggers judicial review immediately, and courts may
substitute their preference for the minority opinion right away.

questions.stem:
In 2025, the President appoints a new Election Commissioner after receiving
recommendations from the Prime Minister and a Union Minister nominated by him. The
Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha is not consulted despite being in office. A public-
interest petitioner challenges the appointment process as incomplete and claims the
appointment is void. The Union argues the President’s appointment power is independent and
committee procedure is only directory.
Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
Appointment is valid because President appoints independently, and any committee is
advisory only; omission of one member cannot matter legally here today.

options.label: b
options.text:
Appointment is valid because PM’s minister can replace Opposition Leader, and selection
committee may be two-member for convenience always in practice too.

options.label: c
options.text:
Appointment is invalid because it needs recommendation of selection committee: Prime
Minister, Lok Sabha Opposition Leader, and Minister nominated by Prime Minister.

options.label: d
options.text:
Appointment is invalid because Commissioners are chosen only by High Court, so
President lacks power even with a committee at all ever.

questions.stimulus:
XI.	Criminal trespass is defined under Section 329 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (BNS).
According to this provision, a person commits criminal trespass when they enter into or upon
property in the possession of another with the intent to commit an offence, or to intimidate,
insult, or annoy the person in possession of that property. Criminal trespass may also occur
when a person lawfully enters property but subsequently remains there unlawfully with the
intent to intimidate, insult, annoy the possessor, or commit an offence. In simple terms,
criminal trespass involves unauthorised entry into another person’s property or unlawful
remaining on the property with a wrongful intention. The essential ingredients of criminal
trespass include unlawful entry, possession of property by another person, unlawful remaining
even after lawful entry, and the presence of criminal intent. Examples include entering
someone’s private garden or farmland without permission, refusing to leave a place after being
asked to do so, or entering a fenced property without authorisation. The punishment for
criminal trespass under Section 329(3), BNS is imprisonment for up to three months, or a fine
up to %5,000, or both.
House trespass is a more serious form of criminal trespass and is defined under Section 330 of
the BNS. The concepts of house-trespass and house-breaking are dealt with in Section 330,
BNS. It occurs when criminal trespass is committed by entering or remaining in a building,
tent, or vessel used as a human dwelling, a place of worship, or a place for the custody of
property. House trespass therefore involves intrusion into private or protected spaces such as
homes, offices, religious institutions, or storage facilities. Even introducing any part of the
body, such as a hand through a window, may amount to house trespass. Examples include
breaking into someone’s house without permission, entering an office building with the
intention of committing theft, or unlawfully entering a temple, mosque, or church. The
punishment for house trespass under Section 329(4), BNS is imprisonment for up to one year,
or a fine up to 75,000, or both. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The key difference between criminal trespass and house trespass lies in the nature of the
property involved. Criminal trespass may occur on any property, including open land or fenced
areas, whereas house trespass specifically involves buildings or structures used for dwelling,
worship, or storage. Both offences require the same intent to commit an offence or to
intimidate, insult, or annoy the possessor, but house trespass is treated as more serious
because it invades spaces associated with privacy and security. More aggravated forms also
exist, such as house-breaking, which is now covered under Section 330, BNS, and punishment
for lurking house-trespass or house-breaking is dealt with under Section 331, BNS. [Word
Count: 448]

questions.stem:
Rohit enters Neha’s clinic during visiting hours to ask about a bill dispute. After the
discussion ends, Neha asks him to leave. Rohit refuses, stands near the reception, loudly
abuses Neha, and says he will stay “to teach her a lesson.” Patients start leaving, and Neha
calls the police. Rohit claims he entered lawfully and cannot be booked for trespass.
Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
No offence because he entered with permission and later quarrelled; lawful entry cannot
convert into trespass at all under law.

options.label: b
options.text:
House trespass because any refusal to leave a shop is treated as entry into a dwelling and
attracts higher penalty.

options.label: c
options.text:
Offence as he lawfully enters property but subsequently remains there unlawfully with
intent to intimidate, insult, or annoy.

options.label: d
options.text:
Mere civil wrong because intent to intimidate or annoy is absent unless he threatens
harm; insults alone are irrelevant here.

questions.stem:
At midnight, Pawan climbs over a locked gate into Amina’s fenced farm. He does not damage
crops or steal anything. Instead, he shouts insults about Amina’s family and stays for ten
minutes to “humiliate her” before leaving. Pawan argues that since nothing was taken, the
matter is only a civil trespass. Amina claims the entry itself was criminal due to the intention.
Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
Criminal Trespass as he enters into or upon property in the possession of another with
intent to intimidate, insult, or annoy the possessor.

options.label: b
options.text:
Not trespass because, without theft or violence entry onto farmland is harmless and only
invites civil suit for damages alone.

options.label: c
options.text:
House trespass because farmland is treated as a place for custody of property so any entry
becomes house trespass automatically.

options.label: d
options.text:
Not trespass because the land was vacant and owner absent; possession requires physical
presence not legal control at night always.

questions.stem:
A courier company stores high-value parcels in a locked warehouse. Late at night, Sameer
enters the warehouse without permission and starts checking boxes, hoping to find expensive
electronics. He is caught before removing any parcel. Sameer argues it is not “house trespass”
because the place is not a home and no one lives there. The prosecution claims the structure is
protected.
Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: a
options.text:
It is house trespass because any entry into any building is house trespass even without
intent to commit offence there.

options.label: b
options.text:
It is only criminal trespass because warehouses are not dwellings worship places or
custody places, so house trespass fails here.

options.label: c
options.text:
No trespass because an unlocked door implies consent, and criminal intent cannot create
liability when entry is permitted at all.

options.label: d
options.text:
It is house trespass because he entered a building used for the custody of property with
criminal intent at night.

Two incidents occur on the same night. First, Ritu climbs into a neighbour’s open backyard to
shout abuses and leave after five minutes. Second, she walks into the neighbour’s locked store-
room attached to the house and searches drawers to “annoy the owner.” Ritu argues both are
the same offence because intention is identical. The owner says the law treats the store-room
intrusion as more serious because of the space invaded.
Which statement best explains the distinction?

options.text:
The key difference lies in the nature of the property involved: open land suits criminal
trespass, buildings suit house trespass.

options.text:
The key difference lies in the nature of the property involved: buildings suit criminal
trespass, open land suits house trespass.

Key difference lies in intent since both apply to any property if annoyance exists, making
building irrelevant always in law.

Key difference lies in ownership since house trespass needs owner possession, but criminal
trespass needs tenant possession only under law.

rather than through religious rituals.

living spouse, both parties must have the mental capacity to give valid consent, the male must
have completed 21 years and the female 18 years, and the parties must not fall within
prohibited degrees of relationship unless permitted by custom. The procedure for marriage

XIII. A quasi-contract is a legal remedy developed by courts to address situations where one party is
unjustly enriched at the expense of another, even though there is no formal agreement or
mutual consent between the parties. The term “quasi” comes from Latin meaning “as if,” and
therefore a quasi-contract is treated as if it were a contract despite lacking essential elements
such as offer, acceptance and consideration. Quasi-contractual obligations are imposed by law
to prevent unfair benefit and ensure that no individual gains at the expense of another. These
obligations are involuntary and arise without the intention of the parties, and their main
objective is restitution, which restores the aggrieved party to the position they were in before
the unjust enrichment occurred.
The key features of quasi-contracts include the absence of agreement between the parties, the
fact that they are imposed by law rather than created by consent, and the remedy of
restitution to compensate the party who suffered loss. The doctrine underlying quasi-contracts
is the doctrine of unjust enrichment, expressed in the maxim “Nemo debet locupletari ex
aliena jactura,” meaning no one should be enriched at another’s expense. In India, quasi-
contracts are codified under Sections 68 to 72 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Section 68
deals with necessaries supplied to a person incapable of contracting, such as a minor, where
reimbursement can be claimed from the person’s property. Section 69 provides that a person
who pays money on behalf of another to protect their own interest is entitled to
reimbursement. Section 70 states that when a person lawfully provides goods or services
without intending them to be gratuitous and the other party benefits, the recipient must
compensate for the benefit. Section 71 imposes responsibility on a finder of goods to take
reasonable care and return them to the rightful owner. Section 72 provides that money paid by
mistake or under coercion must be returned.

The concept evolved from English common law and was articulated in the landmark case of
Moses v. MacFarlane (1760), where Lord Mansfield emphasised the obligation to refund
money received unjustly. Indian courts have also recognised this principle in cases such as
State of Madhya Pradesh v. Bhailal Bhai (1964) and Hari Ram Sheth Khandsari v.
Commissioner of Sales Tax (1958), where restitution was ordered for money paid by mistake.
Unlike express contracts which are based on mutual consent and clearly defined terms, quasi-
contracts are imposed by law and apply only in limited situations to prevent unjust
enrichment. [Word Count: 413]

XIV. Remedies for torts are broadly classified into judicial remedies and extra-judicial remedies.
Judicial remedies are those granted by courts of law to an aggrieved party, while extra-judicial
remedies are those where the injured party lawfully takes action without approaching the
court. The three principal judicial remedies are damages, injunction, and specific restitution of
property. Damages are the primary remedy in tort law and consist of monetary compensation
paid to restore the plaintiff, as far as money can, to the position they would have occupied had
the tort not occurred. Different types of damages are recognised: nominal damages where a
legal right is violated without actual loss, as in Ashby v. White and Constantine v. Imperial
London Hotels Ltd.; contemptuous damages where actual harm is trivial; compensatory
damages to restore actual loss; aggravated damages for additional injury such as humiliation,
pain, and loss of self-esteem; punitive or exemplary damages to punish the defendant and
deter similar conduct; and general and special damages, where general damages flow
naturally from the wrong while special damages must be specifically proved. However, only
damage that is not too remote is compensable, and courts apply principles of remoteness as
seen in Re Polemis and Liesbosch Dredger v. SS Edison.
Another important judicial remedy is injunction, which is an equitable remedy granted at the
discretion of the court. Instead of merely awarding money, the court restrains a person from
continuing a wrongful act or directs them to perform a positive act to undo the wrong.
Injunctions may be temporary or permanent, and mandatory or prohibitory, and are governed
by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and Sections 37 to 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. In
M/s Hindustan Pencils Pvt. Ltd. v. India Stationery Products, injunction was granted to
restrain trademark infringement. The third judicial remedy is specific restitution of property,
which restores goods or property wrongfully taken from the owner.
Extra-judicial remedies allow a person to protect or recover their rights without court
intervention. These include expulsion of a trespasser, re-entry on land, re-caption of goods,
abatement of nuisance, and distress damage feasant, where a person may retain cattle or
beasts that have entered and damaged their property until compensation is made. These
remedies are lawful only if exercised reasonably according to the circumstances. [Word Count:
379]

Every night, a factory runs a loud generator next to Rupa’s apartment, causing sleep loss and
headaches. The factory offers 5,000 per month to “settle” but refuses to shift the generator.
Rupa wants the noise to stop, not just payment, and she approaches the court seeking a
remedy that restrains the wrongful act rather than merely compensating her repeatedly. The
factory argues she should accept money and move on.
What is the most suitable remedy to seek in court?

options.label: a
options.text:
Award only nominal damages, because injunctions are unavailable for continuing wrongs,
and money always suffices in tort law.

options.label: b
options.text:
Order punitive damages, because punishment deters noise, and equitable restraint is
barred where plaintiff can sue repeatedly later.

options.label: c
options.text:
Consider an injunction, an equitable remedy granted at the discretion of the court, to
restrain continuing conduct here.

options.label: d
options.text:
Allow abatement without court, because self-help always preferred, and equitable
remedies require no judicial supervision or order ever.

XIV. Remedies for torts are broadly classified into judicial remedies and extra-judicial remedies.
Judicial remedies are those granted by courts of law to an aggrieved party, while extra-judicial
remedies are those where the injured party lawfully takes action without approaching the
court. The three principal judicial remedies are damages, injunction, and specific restitution of
property. Damages are the primary remedy in tort law and consist of monetary compensation
paid to restore the plaintiff, as far as money can, to the position they would have occupied had
the tort not occurred. Different types of damages are recognised: nominal damages where a
legal right is violated without actual loss, as in Ashby v. White and Constantine v. Imperial
London Hotels Ltd.; contemptuous damages where actual harm is trivial; compensatory
damages to restore actual loss; aggravated damages for additional injury such as humiliation,
pain, and loss of self-esteem; punitive or exemplary damages to punish the defendant and
deter similar conduct; and general and special damages, where general damages flow
naturally from the wrong while special damages must be specifically proved. However, only
damage that is not too remote is compensable, and courts apply principles of remoteness as
seen in Re Polemis and Liesbosch Dredger v. SS Edison.
Another important judicial remedy is injunction, which is an equitable remedy granted at the
discretion of the court. Instead of merely awarding money, the court restrains a person from
continuing a wrongful act or directs them to perform a positive act to undo the wrong.
Injunctions may be temporary or permanent, and mandatory or prohibitory, and are governed
by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and Sections 37 to 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963. In
M/s Hindustan Pencils Pvt. Ltd. v. India Stationery Products, injunction was granted to
restrain trademark infringement. The third judicial remedy is specific restitution of property,
which restores goods or property wrongfully taken from the owner.
Extra-judicial remedies allow a person to protect or recover their rights without court
intervention. These include expulsion of a trespasser, re-entry on land, re-caption of goods,
abatement of nuisance, and distress damage feasant, where a person may retain cattle or
beasts that have entered and damaged their property until compensation is made. These
remedies are lawful only if exercised reasonably according to the circumstances. [Word Count:
379]

compensation can be granted ever.

options.label: d

Seek extra-judicial recaption, because brand misuse is trespass, and self-help seizure
replaces court injunction remedies today always here.

questions.stem:
Gopal finds a neighbour’s cattle repeatedly entering his field and damaging crops. In anger, he
captures the cattle, ties them in a shed, and refuses to release them unless the neighbour pays
a very high amount. When the neighbour comes to negotiate, Gopal pushes him and threatens
to keep the cattle for weeks. The neighbour complains that this is unlawful self-help. Gopal
argues he can retain the cattle until compensation is made.
When is such self-help legally permissible?

options.label: a
options.text:
It is lawful only if exercised reasonably according to the circumstances, so excessive force
or demands defeat it.

options.label: b
options.text:
It is lawful whenever property is invaded, because self-help remedies are absolute rights
and need no restraint ever.

options.label: c
options.text:
It is lawful only after police permission, because extra-judicial acts are illegal unless
authorised by magistrate order first.

options.label: d
options.text:
It is unlawful because courts alone may grant remedies, and private detention of cattle is
always a crime.

SECTION IV
XV. The Union Budget 2026-27 proposes to build a ‘strong care ecosystem’ by training 1.5 lakh
multiskilled caregivers in geriatric, core care and allied skills through programmes aligned
with the National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF). As India’s care needs expand, such
a move is both timely and necessary. However, the Budget reveals a deeper paradox; even as
the state prepares to train a new cadre of certified care professionals, it makes little mention
of the five million plus women who already run India’s health, nutrition and childcare
systems. Our Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs), Anganwadi workers and helpers,
and mid-day meal workers continue to deliver essential public services every day, yet remain
classified as ‘volunteers’, excluded from the very ecosystem the state now seems determined to
strengthen. From the Anganwadi worker ensuring a child is fed to the ASHA worker tracking
a pregnancy in a remote village, these women constitute the backbone of India’s welfare
architecture. Their work is essential, continuous and indispensable to the state, yet they
labour in a deeply precarious space, earning meagre monthly honorariums, without formal
contracts, paid leaves or maternity benefits. What little support they receive comes from small
and fragmented responses by individual States such as honorarium hikes (which vary from
State to State) and gratuity benefits, or coverage under national schemes such as Ayushman
Bharat and Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maandhan. But these piecemeal measures do little to
address the contradiction that lies at the core of India’s care economy — that the state relies
on a vast, feminised shadow labour force of women to deliver essential public services but
classifies them as ‘honorary workers’ to limit protections typically associated with formal
employment.
This contradiction is rooted in deeper structural norms surrounding care. The ‘care penalty’ in
India is not just a sociological concept, it is a statistical reality. Insights from the 2024 Time
Use Survey highlighted in the Economic Survey 2025-26 reinforce Indian women’s role as
primary caregivers, with 41% of females aged 15-59 spending 140 minutes daily on household
caregiving, compared to just 21.4% of males at 74 minutes. This pattern mirrors India’s
welfare architecture. By outsourcing its care responsibilities to women labelled as ‘volunteers’,
the state draws on long-standing social norms that view care work as an extension of a
woman’s domestic duty rather than skilled labour deserving fair compensation. Since care is
seen as ‘natural’ to women, it is rendered cheap and informal. This creates a vicious cycle —
the less care work is recognised as skilled, the less compulsion there is to pay for it, trapping a
predominantly female workforce in insecure employment.
[Word Count: 432]

XVI. Most of America “springs forward” Sunday for daylight saving time. Losing that hour of sleep
can do more than leave you tired and cranky the next day; it also could harm your health.
Darker mornings and more evening light knock your body clock out of whack — which means
daylight saving time can usher in sleep trouble for weeks or longer. Studies have even found
an uptick in heart attacks and strokes right after the March time change. There are ways to
ease the adjustment, including getting more sunshine to help reset your circadian rhythm for
healthful sleep.
Daylight saving time begins Sunday at 2 a.m., an hour of sleep vanishing in most of the U.S.
The ritual will reverse on Nov. 1 when clocks “fall back” as daylight saving time ends. Hawaii
and most of Arizona don’t make the spring switch, sticking to standard time year-round —
along with Puerto Rico, American Samoa, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands. Worldwide,
dozens of countries also observe daylight saving time, starting and ending at different dates.
Some people try to prepare for daylight saving time by going to bed a little earlier two or three
nights ahead. While getting back on schedule after an hour’s change may not be that difficult
for some people, it’s an added challenge for the third of U.S. adults who already don’t get the
recommended seven hours of nightly shuteye. The brain has a master clock that is set by
exposure to sunlight and darkness. This circadian rhythm is a roughly 24-hour cycle that
determines when we become sleepy and when we're more alert. The patterns change with age,
one reason that early-to-rise youngsters evolve into hard-to-wake teens.
Morning light resets the rhythm. By evening, levels of a hormone called melatonin begin to
surge, triggering drowsiness. Too much light in the evening — that extra hour from daylight
saving time — delays that surge and the cycle gets out of sync. Sleep deprivation is linked to
heart disease, cognitive decline, obesity and numerous other problems. And that circadian
clock affects more than sleep, also influencing things like heart rate, blood pressure, stress
hormones and metabolism. Fatal car crashes temporarily jump the first few days after the
spring time change, according to a study of U.S. traffic fatalities. The risk was highest in the
morning, and researchers attributed it to sleep deprivation. Then there’s the cardiac

questions.stimulus:
XVII. Human identity is a captivating and intricate subject. One could argue that with the
emergence of digital platforms, and the widespread availability of more diverse media,
literature and learning opportunities than ever before, the way the average person defines
themselves has undergone a significant transformation. Unlike just a couple of decades ago,
when identity was often linked to one’s personal traits and role within one’s community, today
it is becoming increasingly entangled with the things we consume, especially online.
A compelling case study of this identity shift can be observed in TikTok culture. While trends
on this app emerge in a manner similar to trends spread through magazines and television in
the past (albeit at an incredibly accelerated pace), what’s striking on TikTok is how its users’
sense of themselves is increasingly intertwined with the clothes they wear, the media they
engage with, even the food they eat. Though the notion of products shaping identities was
famously propagated by Edward Bernays, the ‘father of public relations’, way back in the
1920s, this does underscore his profound understanding of human behavior.
Today it’s challenging to find individuals who primarily define themselves by their intrinsic
traits; instead, many tend to define themselves by what they consume. But alongside
straightforward promotion of the products themselves, there’s now a more subtle and insidious
marketing approach at play. These trends are strategically targeted towards women by
associating a particular combination of products with a particular type of woman. For

instance, a trend emerged wherein a mix of various new products, including specific clothing,
jewelry, and branded hair and makeup products, were promoted simultaneously. They were
marketed under the guise of the ‘clean girl’ trend. A ‘clean girl’ is essentially the kind of
woman who consistently appears well-groomed and put together, emanates a pleasant
fragrance, and boasts fresh, radiant skin. The marketing extends beyond the immediate
attributes of the products themselves: it represents an effort to emulate the image of the clean
girl, which is associated with a well-off, high-class lifestyle and a harmonious family
background. So this and other such approaches can be seen as a means for individuals to role-
play various personas they aspire to embody through the use of these products. This
transformation gives rise to a paradox: if individuals are so eager to distinguish themselves
from the crowd, why do they engage in these carefully orchestrated trends that essentially
commodify their identity, categorising them through consumerism? www.lawpreptutorial.com
The straightforward response is capitalism. Capitalism has wrought a profound shift in the
way we perceive ourselves and others. In a world driven by consumerism, competition and
envy, people are increasingly inclined to shape themselves into marketable entities by
endeavoring to make their identities palatable to a wide audience. [Word Count: 453]

questions.stimulus:
XVII. Human identity is a captivating and intricate subject. One could argue that with the
emergence of digital platforms, and the widespread availability of more diverse media,
literature and learning opportunities than ever before, the way the average person defines
themselves has undergone a significant transformation. Unlike just a couple of decades ago,
when identity was often linked to one’s personal traits and role within one’s community, today
it is becoming increasingly entangled with the things we consume, especially online.
A compelling case study of this identity shift can be observed in TikTok culture. While trends
on this app emerge in a manner similar to trends spread through magazines and television in
the past (albeit at an incredibly accelerated pace), what’s striking on TikTok is how its users’
sense of themselves is increasingly intertwined with the clothes they wear, the media they
engage with, even the food they eat. Though the notion of products shaping identities was
famously propagated by Edward Bernays, the ‘father of public relations’, way back in the
1920s, this does underscore his profound understanding of human behavior.
Today it’s challenging to find individuals who primarily define themselves by their intrinsic
traits; instead, many tend to define themselves by what they consume. But alongside
straightforward promotion of the products themselves, there’s now a more subtle and insidious
marketing approach at play. These trends are strategically targeted towards women by
associating a particular combination of products with a particular type of woman. For

instance, a trend emerged wherein a mix of various new products, including specific clothing,
jewelry, and branded hair and makeup products, were promoted simultaneously. They were
marketed under the guise of the ‘clean girl’ trend. A ‘clean girl’ is essentially the kind of
woman who consistently appears well-groomed and put together, emanates a pleasant
fragrance, and boasts fresh, radiant skin. The marketing extends beyond the immediate
attributes of the products themselves: it represents an effort to emulate the image of the clean
girl, which is associated with a well-off, high-class lifestyle and a harmonious family
background. So this and other such approaches can be seen as a means for individuals to role-
play various personas they aspire to embody through the use of these products. This
transformation gives rise to a paradox: if individuals are so eager to distinguish themselves
from the crowd, why do they engage in these carefully orchestrated trends that essentially
commodify their identity, categorising them through consumerism? www.lawpreptutorial.com
The straightforward response is capitalism. Capitalism has wrought a profound shift in the
way we perceive ourselves and others. In a world driven by consumerism, competition and
envy, people are increasingly inclined to shape themselves into marketable entities by
endeavoring to make their identities palatable to a wide audience. [Word Count: 453]
